To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed a novel cAMP BERT biosensor to investigate the activity of putatively endogenous ligands of trace amine receptors and that we have shown that trace amine receptors are expressed at the cell surface when a glycosylation site is added to their N-terminal domain.

the addition of a glycosylation site at the N terminus to the human trace amide receptor 1 (human TAAR1) enables its plasma membrane expression and pharmacological characterization using a novel cAMP bioluminescence energy transfer (BETT) biosensor.

the addition of a glycosylation site at the N terminus to the human TAAR1 enables its membrane expression in HEK 293 cells and allows for its pharmacological characterization using a BRET based cAMP biosensor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel cAMP BRT assay that is capable of identifying ligands for poorly expressing GPCRS.
the identification of novel pharmacological agents to modulate the activity of trace amine-associated receptors (TAAR) and their downstream signaling pathways.

the identification and characterization of novel ligands that bind to trace amine associated G protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), and the development of a novel cAMP bioluminescent resonance energy transfer (cAMP BRET) biosensor that can be applied to the study of poorly expressing GPCR systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TAAR1 is a novel GPCR, which is expressed on the surface of cells and is coupled to a G-protein, which is able to activate adenylyl cyclase.
the addition of a glycosylation site is sufficient to enable the membrane expression of TAARs, and thus their pharmacological characterization with an EPAC-based BRET biosensor.
TAAR1 is a GPCR that can be pharmacologically activated by trace amines.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a strategy to express and characterize a novel GPCR, TAAR1, and have identified a number of putative TAARI ligands.
we were able to identify a novel strategy to express TAARS, and to characterize them using a cAMP biosensor.

we have developed a novel strategy to identify the ligands of a family of poorly expressed GPCRs that could be used for the pharmacological characterization of many GPCRs that are difficult to express in model systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the addition of a glycosylation site is sufficient to enable the expression of TAAR1 in model cell systems.
TAAR1 can be expressed in a functional state in a mammalian cell system, allowing for a more thorough characterization of its ligand binding and signaling properties.
TAAR1, a poorly expressing GPCR, can be expressed at the cell surface and pharmacologically profiled by a cAMP BERT biosensor.
